The Chilean sea urchin Loxechinus albus begins life as a fertilized egg of relatively modest dimensions, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0000005 grams [Wwb = 0.0000005 grams], a value derived from the roughly 1-millimeter diameter of the ovum following external fertilisation. Developing through a planktotrophic pluteus larva, these free-swimming individuals feed actively on phytoplankton as they grow within the water column. The larval phase culminates in metamorphosis, a dramatic morphological transformation involving arm resorption and substratum attachment. Upon completion of this larval-juvenile transition, the recently metamorphosed juvenile emerges at a body length of 0.09 centimeters  and a wet weight of 0.00048 grams . These marked shifts in size and form accompany the shift from a bilateral larval body plan to the pentaradial symmetry of the juvenile sea urchin, allowing the young post-metamorphic individual to begin grazing on benthic algae in its rocky subtidal habitat.

Sexual maturation in Loxechinus albus proceeds gradually, with the onset of gametogenesis occurring only after individuals have attained a test diameter of 4.3 centimeters [Lp = 4.3 centimeters]. At this pubertal milestone, the wet weight of the animal typically reaches 33 grams [Wwp = 33 grams], reflecting considerable somatic investment in the calcareous test and associated soft tissues prior to reproductive activation. Puberty in this species thus represents a threshold where energetic resources begin to be partitioned toward gonad maturation alongside continued skeletal growth. In the context of the cold-temperate waters of the southeastern Pacific, where water temperatures hover around 11 °C [T = 11 °C] for much of the year, this length at puberty is attained after a prolonged juvenile phase that may span several years. The timing of this transition is influenced by local food availability and density-dependent competition, factors that can accelerate or delay the onset of gonadal activity by several months across different populations.

For reproductively active adults of Loxechinus albus maintained under typical thermal conditions of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the maximum reproductive output is expressed through a combination of moderate fecundity per spawning event and a defined seasonal frequency. Gravid individuals release approximately 55,000 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = approximately 55,000 eggs per spawning], and a single female can participate in roughly one such spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one such spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive output, while not exceptionally high among echinoids, reflects a life-history strategy that balances gamete production with the energetic costs of maintaining test integrity and feeding apparatus function in a resource-variable kelp forest environment. The spawning season is synchronized with phytoplankton blooms that provide food for the resulting planktotrophic larvae, underscoring the tight coupling between reproductive timing and environmental productivity gradients.

Adult body size in Loxechinus albus exhibits a well-defined upper boundary, with the ultimate test diameter recorded at 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters] in large, presumably older individuals from productive Chilean beds. Corresponding to this maximum test size, the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 490 grams [Wwi = approximately 490 grams], a mass that includes the robust calcareous test, the Aristotle's lantern, and well-developed gonadal tissue. These asymptotic dimensions are consistent with those reported for other large echinoids in the family Echinidae, though Loxechinus albus tends toward slightly larger test diameters than its North Atlantic congener Echinus esculentus. Achieving such size requires sustained access to abundant macroalgae, primarily Macrocystis pyrifera, over many years of continuous feeding. The relationship between test diameter and wet weight follows a power-law scaling, with the heaviest individuals typically dominating the most productive, wave-exposed habitats where food is least limiting.

The maximum lifespan documented for Loxechinus albus under natural conditions in the cold waters of the Chilean fjord region, where temperatures remain near 11 °C [T = 11 °C] year-round, is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This longevity is notable among sea urchins and is thought to be linked to the species' relatively slow growth rate at low ambient temperatures, combined with low natural predation pressure in deeper rocky reefs. Senescence in this species is characterized by progressive deterioration of the feeding apparatus and a gradual decline in gonadal output, with very old individuals eventually exhibiting reduced mobility and eroded test plates. Temperature appears to play a modulating role, with individuals from warmer northern populations potentially exhibiting shorter lifespans than those from colder southern refugia.
